analysis.summary:
gemini-3.5-flash-lite: Multiple independent studies and reports indicate that utility-scale solar has become the cheapest source of electricity in most markets and countries, falling below fossil fuels like coal and natural gas. However, integration and grid infrastructure challenges, such as bidirectional rooftop solar flows, can introduce localized costs and affect overall utility spending.
groq-gpt-oss-120b: Recent reports say solar power often costs less than coal or gas to generate, but other research shows adding solar can raise overall electricity bills because of grid upgrades and policy costs. The evidence is mixed, so it’s unclear if solar is always the cheapest option.
verify_yourself: Check the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) reports published annually by organizations like Lazard.
Review empirical literature from MIT CEEPR regarding utility spending and residential electricity prices.
Compare the latest International Energy Agency (IEA) LCOE report with the MIT studies on grid integration costs to see which cost metric dominates overall electricity pricing.
Open at least two sources of different types (e.g. a research paper and a news report) and read past the headline.
Check who wrote or paid for each source, and whether they gain from you believing it.
Look for the original data or document (study, law, official record) instead of someone describing it.
Search the claim on a fact-checker like Snopes, PolitiFact, or FactCheck.org.
Check the date - old facts can be out of date.

Different methods of electricity generation can incur a variety of different costs, which can be divided into three general categories: 1) wholesale costs, or all costs paid by utilities associated with acquiring and distributing electricity to consumers, 2) retail costs paid by consumers, and 3) external costs, or externalities, imposed on society.
Wholesale costs include initial capital, operations and maintenance (O&M), transmission, and costs of decommissioning. Depending on the local regulatory environment, some or all wholesale costs may be passed through to consumers. These are costs per unit of energy, typically represented as dollars/megawatt hour (wholesale). The calculations also assist governments in making decisions regarding energy policy.

Renewable energy (also called green energy) is energy made from renewable natural resources that are replenished on a human timescale. The most widely used renewable energy types are solar energy, wind power, bioenergy/biomass, and hydropower. Bioenergy and geothermal power are also significant in some countries. The study, published in Energy and Environmental Materials by the university’s Advanced Technology Institute (ATI), reveals that solar photovoltaic (PV) technology is not only affordable but also rapidly becoming the driving force behind the global shift toward clean and renewable energy. As countries around the world race to reduce carbon emissions and combat climate change, the plummeting cost of solar power is positioning it at the forefront of a sustainable energy revolution, making green energy accessible on an unprecedented scale. Professor Ravi Silva, co-author of the study and Director of the ATI, emphasised the growing affordability of solar power: “Even in the UK, located 50 degrees north of the equator, solar has become the most cost-effective option for large-scale electricity generation. Worldwide, installed solar capacity surpassed 1.5 terawatts in 2024, double the level seen in 2020, enough to supply power to hundreds of millions of homes. This demonstrates that solar is no longer an experimental or futuristic concept; it has become a cornerstone of the resilient, low-carbon energy future we are striving to achieve.” The study also underscores a dramatic drop in the cost of lithium-ion batteries, which have fallen by 89% since 2010. sources.text: Solar power became the most affordable energy source between 2021 and 2025, with costs dropping below coal and natural gas in most regions. Solar power has taken center stage in the clean energy race. By 2025, sunlight powers cities, industries, and homes across continents. The shift began quietly in 2021, but now it defines global energy systems. Research from the University of Surrey shows solar energy driving both climate action and economic growth. Every continent now invests heavily in solar technology. Farmers install small PV panels. Corporations build massive solar farms . People see sunlight not as a free gift but as a daily resource. From 2021 to 2025, solar capacity grew faster than any other renewable source. China dominates installation numbers, followed by India’s expanding solar zones. Europe’s rooftops glitter with panels, while American companies power data centers with clean energy . Falling prices and supportive policies fuel this momentum. Governments simplify permits. Banks create green loans. Communities embrace local solar cooperatives. Even remote villages now power schools and hospitals using solar grids. In less than five years, solar has moved from ambition to habit. What once seemed futuristic now defines normal life. The turning point came when the levelized cost of electricity for solar dropped sharply. Today, solar electricity costs less than $20 per megawatt-hour in several regions. sources.text: Energy prices nationwide have been rising at roughly twice the rate of inflation. Many observers link this trend to the rapid growth of renewable generators, particularly utility-scale wind and solar. This has contributed to the recissions of the incentives and policies that previously helped renewables account for over 80% of new U.S. generation capacity in 2024 (FERC 2025). Prior studies argue that RPSs can raise electricity prices by imposing high compliance costs on utilities in certain states (Wiser 2025). Building on this literature, this paper uses a fixed-effects econometric approach to estimate plausibly causal effects of RPSs and renewable generation on residential electricity prices and utility expenditures over time and across states. We draw upon data from the Energy Information Administration, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, and the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory to construct a state-utility year panel dataset that links residential electricity prices, RPSs, generation mixes, and utility spending. We focus our analysis on the most recent 25 years of complete data from 1998 through 2023. This dataset enables us to address two crucial questions: to what extent can we attribute increases in residential electricity prices to a decarbonizing electricity sector, and how does greater renewable generation impact utility spending? sources.text: CAMBRIDGE, Mass., March 9, 2026 – In the last year, energy costs rose at triple the rate of overall inflation , the latest spike in a decades-long trend that has seen utility bills consistently outpace the cost of living. Some policymakers blame renewable energy mandates for the surge, while others emphasize that investment in renewables creates cheaper electricity because of its low production costs — but new research from the MIT Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research (CEEPR) suggests that the truth is more complicated. MIT Sloan professor Christopher R. Knittel and graduate researcher Fischer J. Espiritu Argosino address this issue in a new working paper, “ Renewables and Electricity Affordability: Untangling Correlation from Causation ,”  where they analyze 25 years of U.S. electricity and utility spending data. They find that while utility-scale wind and solar are robustly linked to lower residential prices, rooftop solar is significantly correlated with higher prices. The study, based on data from 1998 through 2023, examines residential prices, state power generation mixes, utility spending, and state Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS) — mandates requiring a portion of energy to come from green sources. sources.text: Module prices fell again in 2026, pushing utility-scale solar below new coal and gas in more than 80 countries. Grid connection queues, not cost, are the main constraint. By Dr. Anya Raman · July 28, 2026 · 6 min read · Updated July 30, 2026 Levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) measures the average cost of generating one megawatt-hour over a plant's lifetime. On this measure, utility-scale solar has fallen faster than any other generation technology over the past decade, driven by manufacturing scale, higher cell efficiency, and cheaper capital equipment. In most markets with reasonable irradiance, a new solar plant now produces electricity at a lower cost than a newly built coal or gas plant, even before carbon pricing is applied. Where solar is paired with battery storage, the combined cost is competitive with new gas peaking capacity in a growing number of grids. Falling costs have shifted the constraint from economics to infrastructure. Interconnection queues in Europe, the United States, and India now hold multiples of the capacity that is actually built each year, because transmission planning and grid upgrades run on longer timelines than solar construction.
